narration.heading: Kicked out
narration.text: You were taught there were nine planets? Meet the worlds that got kicked out.

narration.heading: Ceres
narration.text: Ceres was called a planet for half a century. It holds about forty percent of the asteroid belt's mass.

narration.heading: Makemake
narration.text: Way out past Neptune, Makemake. It's named after a creator god of the Rapa Nui people of Easter Island.

narration.heading: Eris
narration.text: Then Eris, found in 2005. It's more massive than Pluto, and it started all the trouble.

narration.heading: The vote
narration.text: Astronomers had to decide what a planet even is. In 2006, they voted.

narration.heading: Pluto
narration.text: Pluto, discovered in 1930, became a dwarf planet. It's still the biggest one, though, by a hair.

narration.heading: Our Moon
narration.text: Now our own Moon, about three thousand five hundred kilometres across.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: The twist? Pluto is smaller than our Moon, with just a sixth of its mass.

narration.heading: Your vote
narration.text: So should Pluto be a planet again? Planet, or not? Tell us in the comments.

hook.banner: Why did Pluto stop being a planet?

skit.text: Kicked out for being small? Pluto, I'm one line of code. I feel you.

titles: What if you lined up the planets that got demoted?
The dwarf planets, to scale, next to our Moon
youtube.description: Ceres, Makemake, Eris and Pluto side by side at true scale, why Pluto lost its planet status in 2006, and how it compares with our own Moon.

sources.claim: Ceres has a mean radius of about 469.7 km (about 939 km across), was listed as a planet for over half a century, and holds about 40% of the asteroid belt's mass
Makemake, in the Kuiper belt beyond Neptune, has a mean radius of 715 km and is named after the creator god of the Rapa Nui people of Easter Island
Eris, discovered in 2005, is about 2,326 km across and about 27% more massive than Pluto; its size prompted the IAU to define 'planet', approved on 24 August 2006

Pluto, discovered in 1930, has a mean radius of 1,188.3 km (2,376.6 km across), became a dwarf planet under the 2006 IAU definition, is the largest known dwarf planet by volume, and has about one-sixth the Moon's mass
The Moon's mean radius is 1,737.4 km (about 3,475 km across)
